source.title: Adjuvant Pembrolizumab after Nephrectomy in Renal-Cell Carcinoma

extraction_metadata.source_boundary: Primary trial report plus material Supplementary Appendix. Protocol content is used for method reconciliation, not converted into observed results.

atoms.canonical_statement: KEYNOTE-564 evaluated whether adjuvant pembrolizumab after nephrectomy, with or without metastasectomy, improved outcomes versus placebo in clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma at protocol-defined recurrence risk.
Eligible patients were at least 18 years old with histologically confirmed renal-cell carcinoma containing a clear-cell component and protocol-defined high recurrence risk.

population.label: Eligible clear-cell RCC population
inclusion_criteria: Histologically confirmed RCC with a clear-cell component

atoms.canonical_statement: Protocol-defined recurrence risk included pT2 grade 4 or sarcomatoid disease, pT3 or higher disease, regional lymph-node metastasis, or M1 with no evidence of disease.
Patients could not have received prior systemic therapy for renal-cell carcinoma and required negative surgical margins after nephrectomy or metastasectomy within 12 weeks before randomization.

population.label: Surgically treated eligible population
exclusion_criteria: Prior systemic therapy for renal-cell carcinoma

atoms.canonical_statement: For M1 NED eligibility, metastases had to be completely resected at nephrectomy or within 1 year after nephrectomy.

population.label: M1 NED eligible population
inclusion_criteria: Resection at nephrectomy or within 1 year afterward

atoms.canonical_statement: Supplementary exclusions included immunodeficiency, active autoimmune disease, current or prior pneumonitis, active infection requiring systemic therapy, and certain recent active malignancies.
KEYNOTE-564 was an international phase 3 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial with 1:1 treatment assignment.
Randomization was stratified by M0 versus M1 NED status. Within M0, it was further stratified by ECOG performance status 0 versus 1 and United States versus outside the United States.
Patients and investigators were unaware of treatment assignment.
Pembrolizumab was given at 200 mg intravenously once every 3 weeks for up to 17 cycles, approximately 1 year.

exposures.details: Adjuvant therapy after nephrectomy, with or without metastasectomy.

atoms.canonical_statement: The control was intravenous carrier-saline placebo once every 3 weeks for up to 17 cycles, approximately 1 year.

exposures.details: Carrier saline placebo.

atoms.canonical_statement: Treatment could be interrupted or discontinued, but pembrolizumab dose modification was not permitted.
The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed disease-free survival from randomization to first local or distant recurrence or death from any cause.

outcome.definition: Time from randomization to first documented local or distant renal-cell carcinoma recurrence or death from any cause, whichever occurred first.

atoms.canonical_statement: Overall survival, defined as time from randomization to death from any cause, was the key secondary endpoint.

outcome.definition: Time from randomization to death from any cause.

atoms.canonical_statement: Safety and patient-reported outcomes were secondary endpoints.
Efficacy analyses used the intention-to-treat population, while safety analyses used all patients who received at least one dose.
The trial used Kaplan-Meier estimation, stratified log-rank testing, and a stratified Cox model with Efron tie handling for disease-free and overall survival.
The planned disease-free survival analysis assumed about 990 participants and 332 events, with 95% power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.67 at one-sided alpha 2.5%.
Multiplicity used a graphical fixed-sequence approach in which disease-free survival was tested first and alpha passed to overall survival only after a successful disease-free survival test.

The reported interim analysis was prespecified near 265 disease-free survival events with at least 12 months of minimum follow-up; the article reports an actual one-sided significance boundary of 0.0114.
The final overall survival analysis was planned after approximately 200 deaths.
An independent external data and safety monitoring committee reviewed efficacy and safety at the prespecified interim analysis.
Merck participated in trial design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, and manuscript writing.
From 1406 screened patients at 213 sites in 21 countries, 994 were randomized, 496 to pembrolizumab and 498 to placebo.
The as-treated population included 488 pembrolizumab recipients and 496 placebo recipients.
Baseline risk categories were balanced; 86.1% and 86.9% were M0 intermediate-to-high risk, and 5.8% in each arm were M1 NED.
Five participants classified as M0 intermediate-to-high risk had lower-stage disease and were protocol violations.
Among 58 M1 NED participants, two pembrolizumab patients had resected bone metastases and one placebo patient had a resected brain metastasis, all labeled protocol violations.
At the December 14, 2020 cutoff, median time from randomization to cutoff was 24.1 months, range 14.9 to 41.5 months.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that no clinically meaningful changes in either patient-reported outcome instrument were observed and that scores were stable over the trial period.
Numbers at risk beyond the median 24-month follow-up were small, making Kaplan-Meier tail estimates unstable and requiring caution.
Some subgroup analyses had small patient and event counts, so subgroup estimates require caution.
The M1 NED subgroup represented 5.8% of the trial and was too small for definitive interpretation.
Overall survival was immature at cutoff, with only 26% of the deaths prespecified for final analysis observed.
Extended enrollment produced substantial censoring beyond 2 years, and longer follow-up was needed to determine durable cure proportions and overall survival effect.

At the prespecified first interim analysis, the authors concluded that adjuvant pembrolizumab significantly improved disease-free survival versus placebo after surgery in patients at high recurrence risk.
The trial was funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck.
The article states that a data sharing statement was available with the full text at NEJM.org; the statement itself was not present in this Drive packet.
